title: Basic Nursing Care — Specimen Collection & Diagnostic Prep (Set 13)
subtitle: Correct client identification and specimen labeling, clean-catch/midstream urine, 24-hour urine, stool and sputum collection technique, safe handling and timing, culture-before-antibiotics, requisition matching, documentation, and preparing clients for diagnostic tests and procedures
scenario: Collecting specimens accurately and safely and preparing clients for diagnostic tests: verifying identity, using correct technique for each specimen type, handling and labeling properly, and supporting test preparation within the technician's scope.

steps.q: Before collecting any specimen, the technician should FIRST:

opts.text: Verify the client's identity using two identifiers
opts.rat: Confirming identity with two identifiers ensures the specimen is collected from and labeled for the correct client, preventing dangerous mix-ups.

opts.text: Label the container after the client has left
opts.rat: Specimens are labeled at the bedside for the correct client, not later from memory.

opts.text: Collect first and identify the client afterward
opts.rat: Identity must be confirmed before collection to avoid errors.

opts.text: Skip identification if the unit is familiar
opts.rat: Identity is always verified, regardless of familiarity.

steps.q: Specimen containers should be labeled:

opts.text: Accurately at the bedside, matching the client and the requisition, before leaving the room
opts.rat: Labeling at the bedside against the client and order prevents mislabeling, a serious safety error.

opts.text: Later at the nurses' station from memory
opts.rat: Labeling away from the bedside risks mix-ups; it is done at the point of collection.

opts.text: Only if the lab requests it
opts.rat: All specimens are labeled correctly as a standard safety practice.

opts.text: With just the room number
opts.rat: Proper labeling uses client identifiers, not only a room number.

steps.q: A clean-catch (midstream) urine specimen is collected by having the client:

opts.text: Clean the area, begin voiding, then catch urine midstream in a sterile container
opts.rat: Cleaning first and catching the middle of the stream reduces contamination and yields a more accurate result.

opts.text: Collect the very first drops of urine without cleaning
opts.rat: The first stream and an uncleaned area increase contamination; midstream after cleaning is preferred.

opts.text: Urinate into the toilet and scoop from the bowl
opts.rat: Toilet water contaminates the specimen; a sterile container is used.

opts.text: Use any nearby cup without cleaning
opts.rat: A clean-catch requires cleaning and a sterile container to limit contamination.

steps.q: For a 24-hour urine collection, the technician should:

opts.text: Discard the first void to start timing, then collect all urine for 24 hours—including the final void—storing per policy
opts.rat: The collection begins with an empty bladder (first void discarded) and captures all urine over the full period, ending with a final void, kept per storage requirements.

opts.text: Save the first void and stop collecting after one or two samples
opts.rat: The first void is discarded to mark the start, and all urine for the full 24 hours is collected.

opts.text: Collect only urine that appears abnormal
opts.rat: All urine over 24 hours is collected, not selectively.

opts.text: Leave the container at room temperature and open to air regardless of policy
opts.rat: Storage (often refrigerated/on ice) follows policy; ignoring it can invalidate the test.

steps.q: If any urine is accidentally discarded during a 24-hour collection, the technician should:

opts.text: Report it, because a missed sample can invalidate the test and it may need to restart
opts.rat: Completeness is essential; a missed void compromises accuracy, so it is reported and the collection may be restarted per policy.

opts.text: Say nothing and send the incomplete collection
opts.rat: An incomplete collection gives inaccurate results; it must be reported.

opts.text: Add extra water to make up the volume
opts.rat: Adding water falsifies the specimen and is never done.

opts.text: Guess how much was lost and note it
opts.rat: Guessing does not fix a compromised collection; report it.

steps.q: When collecting a stool specimen, the technician should ensure the sample is NOT contaminated with:

opts.text: Urine, toilet water, or toilet paper
opts.rat: Contamination with urine, toilet water, or paper can affect stool test results, so the sample is collected to avoid them.

opts.text: The correct labeling
opts.rat: Proper labeling is required, not something to avoid.

opts.text: A clean collection container
opts.rat: A clean container is used; it is not a contaminant.

opts.text: The client's identification
opts.rat: Client identification is necessary, not a contaminant.

steps.q: A sputum specimen for the lab is best obtained by having the client:

opts.text: Take deep breaths and cough deeply to bring up secretions from the lungs, ideally in the early morning
opts.rat: A deep cough produces true lower-airway sputum rather than saliva, and early-morning samples tend to be more concentrated.

opts.text: Spit ordinary saliva into the cup
opts.rat: Saliva is not sputum; a deep cough is needed for a valid specimen.

opts.text: Provide the sample right after brushing with mouthwash mid-day
opts.rat: Timing and technique matter; a deep morning cough is preferred, and saliva/mouthwash residue is not the target.

opts.text: Clear the throat lightly without coughing
opts.rat: Throat clearing yields saliva, not deep-airway sputum.

steps.q: After a specimen is collected, it should generally be:

opts.text: Sent to the lab promptly or stored as required, not left sitting out
opts.rat: Timely transport or correct storage preserves specimen integrity; delays and improper storage can alter results.

opts.text: Left on the counter for several hours
opts.rat: Leaving specimens out can degrade them and invalidate results.

opts.text: Kept in the client's room overnight
opts.rat: Specimens are transported or stored properly, not kept casually in the room.

opts.text: Discarded and recollected only if the lab complains
opts.rat: Proper handling is done from the start, not after a complaint.

steps.q: When handling any specimen, the technician should use:

opts.text: Standard precautions—gloves, hand hygiene, and a properly closed container
opts.rat: Body-fluid specimens are treated as potentially infectious; standard precautions and secure containment protect staff and others.

opts.text: Bare hands to feel the specimen's temperature
opts.rat: Touching specimens without gloves risks exposure to infectious material.

opts.text: An open, uncovered cup for transport
opts.rat: Specimens are transported in closed containers to prevent spills and exposure.

opts.text: No precautions if the client 'looks healthy'
opts.rat: Standard precautions apply to all specimens regardless of appearance.

steps.q: For a culture specimen (to identify infection), a general principle is that it is best obtained:

opts.text: Using clean/sterile technique and, when possible, before antibiotics are started
opts.rat: Sterile technique prevents contamination, and collecting before antibiotics improves the chance of identifying the organism.

opts.text: After several days of antibiotics for best results
opts.rat: Antibiotics can suppress the organism, making it harder to identify; culture is ideally obtained before starting them.

opts.text: With deliberately contaminated technique
opts.rat: Contamination invalidates a culture; sterile technique is used.

opts.text: Only from a different client for comparison
opts.rat: The specimen must come from the correct client being evaluated.

steps.q: The requisition (test order) that accompanies a specimen should:

opts.text: Match the specimen and the client so the correct test is performed on the right sample
opts.rat: Matching the requisition to the labeled specimen and client ensures the intended test is run on the right sample.

opts.text: Be for any client to save paperwork
opts.rat: The requisition must correspond to the specific client and specimen.

opts.text: Be left blank and filled in by the lab
opts.rat: Required information is provided accurately, not left blank.

opts.text: List a different test than the one ordered
opts.rat: The requisition reflects the actual order to avoid errors.

steps.q: After collecting a specimen, the technician should document:

opts.text: The type of specimen, the date/time collected, its appearance if relevant, and that it was sent to the lab
opts.rat: Clear documentation supports accurate results interpretation and continuity of care.

opts.text: Nothing, since the lab keeps its own records
opts.rat: Collection is documented in the client's record, not left solely to the lab.

opts.text: Only the client's room number
opts.rat: Documentation includes specimen details, not just a room number.

opts.text: A guess about the test result
opts.rat: The technician documents the collection, not a guessed result.

steps.q: Some blood tests or procedures require the client to fast beforehand. The technician should:

opts.text: Follow the specific fasting/NPO order and verify the client has been prepared as directed
opts.rat: Fasting requirements vary by test; following the exact order and confirming preparation ensures valid results and safety.

opts.text: Decide on their own how long the client should fast
opts.rat: Fasting duration follows the order, not the technician's independent decision.

opts.text: Let the client eat freely regardless of the order
opts.rat: Ignoring an NPO order can invalidate the test or create risk.

opts.text: Assume fasting is never needed
opts.rat: Certain tests do require fasting; the order is followed.

steps.q: When a client is scheduled for a diagnostic procedure, part of preparation is to:

opts.text: Reinforce simple explanations, ensure ordered prep is done, support comfort, and confirm required consent was obtained by the appropriate staff
opts.rat: Preparing the client includes reinforcing teaching, completing ordered prep, comfort measures, and confirming that the proper consent process was handled by licensed staff.

opts.text: Obtain the client's informed consent for the procedure independently
opts.rat: Obtaining informed consent for a procedure is the responsibility of the provider performing it, not the technician.

opts.text: Skip preparation to save time
opts.rat: Proper preparation is important for safety and accurate results.

opts.text: Tell the client nothing to avoid worrying them
opts.rat: Appropriate, honest preparation reduces anxiety and supports cooperation.

steps.q: Teaching a client to collect their own specimen correctly is important because:

opts.text: Proper technique reduces contamination and gives more accurate results
opts.rat: Clear instructions help the client collect a valid, uncontaminated specimen, improving accuracy.

opts.text: It does not matter how the client collects it
opts.rat: Technique strongly affects the accuracy of the result.

opts.text: Contaminated specimens give the best results
opts.rat: Contamination reduces accuracy; clean technique is needed.

opts.text: Instructions confuse clients and should be skipped
opts.rat: Clear instructions help, not hinder, correct collection.

steps.q: Two client identifiers used to confirm identity before collection could be:

opts.text: The client's full name and date of birth (per facility policy)
opts.rat: Using two approved identifiers such as name and date of birth reliably confirms the correct client.

opts.text: The room number alone
opts.rat: A room number is not an acceptable client identifier by itself.

opts.text: Whoever is in the bed at the time
opts.rat: Assuming based on bed position risks a serious mix-up.

opts.text: The staff member's own name
opts.rat: Identifiers must belong to the client, not the staff.

steps.q: If the technician notices a specimen looks unusual (for example, urine that is very cloudy or bloody), they should:

opts.text: Document the appearance objectively and report it to the nurse
opts.rat: Objective documentation and reporting of an abnormal appearance support timely evaluation.

opts.text: Diagnose the cause and begin treatment
opts.rat: Diagnosing and treating are outside the technician's scope.

opts.text: Discard it so no one worries
opts.rat: Discarding an abnormal specimen removes important information; it is reported.

opts.text: Ignore it as unimportant
opts.rat: Unusual findings are documented and reported, not ignored.

steps.q: When transporting a client for a diagnostic test, the technician should:

opts.text: Confirm the correct client and test, ensure safety and comfort during transport, and follow any ordered preparation
opts.rat: Verifying identity and the test, transporting safely, and ensuring prep is complete prevent errors and support the client.

opts.text: Take whoever is ready without checking the order
opts.rat: Transporting the wrong client or for the wrong test is a serious error.

opts.text: Ignore the client's comfort and safety
opts.rat: Comfort and safety during transport are part of good care.

opts.text: Skip verifying the test that is scheduled
opts.rat: The scheduled test and client are verified before transport.

steps.q: Collecting the correct specimen at the correct time (for example, a timed sample) matters because:

opts.text: Some tests depend on specific timing, and errors can produce inaccurate or unusable results
opts.rat: Timed and correctly typed specimens are essential for accurate results; wrong timing or type can invalidate the test.

opts.text: Timing never affects test results
opts.rat: Timing is critical for many tests.

opts.text: Any specimen at any time is equally valid
opts.rat: The correct type and timing are required for validity.

opts.text: The lab prefers surprises
opts.rat: Accuracy depends on following the ordered type and timing.

steps.q: Overall, the technician's role in specimen collection and diagnostic prep is to:

opts.text: Collect specimens correctly within scope, verify identity, label and handle them properly, prepare and support clients, and report—leaving diagnosis and consent for procedures to licensed staff
opts.rat: The technician collects accurately, safeguards identity and handling, prepares clients, and reports, while diagnosis and procedure consent belong to licensed providers.

opts.text: Interpret and diagnose the test results
opts.rat: Interpreting and diagnosing are outside the technician's scope.

opts.text: Obtain informed consent for invasive procedures
opts.rat: Informed consent for a procedure is obtained by the provider performing it.

opts.text: Skip labeling and handling standards when busy
opts.rat: Labeling and handling standards are always followed to ensure safety and accuracy.

reference: Aligned to the California BVNPT Psychiatric Technician exam content area: Basic Nursing Care (specimen collection and diagnostic preparation). Written from standard psychiatric-technician and nursing references at an introductory level. Practices are stated conceptually and marked for faculty confirmation: two-identifier verification and bedside labeling; clean-catch/midstream urine; 24-hour urine collection (discard first void, collect all urine including the final void, store per policy, restart if a sample is lost); avoiding contamination of stool specimens; deep-cough (ideally early-morning) sputum vs saliva; prompt transport/proper storage; standard precautions; culture using sterile technique ideally before antibiotics; requisition matching; documentation; fasting/NPO per order; and diagnostic-procedure preparation. Consistent with the technician's scope: collect, handle, prepare, and report, while diagnosis and obtaining informed consent for procedures are performed by licensed staff. No specific fasting durations, storage temperatures, or reference values are asserted. Builds on NPO (bnc-core-05), catheter urine specimen and blood-in-urine reporting (bnc-core-06), and capillary blood glucose (bnc-core-11). Pending faculty review.
